title: UN Climate Talks End Without Deal as Fossil Fuel Language Vanishes
excerpt: COP31 in Turkey wrapped up as the longest UN climate summit ever, but deep splits over fossil fuels and finance left delegates empty‑handed.
body:
The United Nations climate conference in Antalya, Turkey—known as COP31—concluded after a record‑breaking two weeks without a binding political agreement.  Delegates had hoped to finish on Friday, but negotiations spilled into Sunday as they searched for common ground.  In the end, the draft text that emerged failed to satisfy key groups, and the summit became the longest UN climate meeting in history.

## Fossil fuels left off the table
One of the most striking absences in the final draft was any direct mention of "fossil fuels," the primary driver of global warming.  While a nod to the COP28 decision to "transition away" from coal, oil and gas appeared, the words themselves were omitted.  The European Union’s representative, Irish Minister Darragh O’Brien, blasted the text as “unconscionable” for not naming fossil fuels and said it fell far short of the ambition needed.  Pacific island nations, Panama, the Marshall Islands and other vulnerable states echoed the criticism, arguing the pact did not go far enough to curb the climate crisis.

## Money talks fell silent
Another flashpoint was climate finance.  Poorer countries have long pressed for clear commitments from wealthier nations to help them adapt to more intense heatwaves, droughts and sea‑level rise.  Although COP30 in Brazil had secured a pledge to triple adaptation finance, the COP31 draft offered no concrete figures or baseline for measuring progress.  African climate think‑tank Power Shift Africa’s Mohamed Adow warned that rich nations risk walking away empty‑handed, while the UK’s Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh called the failure “immensely disappointing” but reaffirmed the UK’s unwavering commitment.

## Political dynamics and blame
The summit’s political backdrop was anything but smooth.  Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose country co‑hosted the talks, blamed “difficult geopolitical times” for the deadlock.  Meanwhile, UN Secretary‑General Antonio Guterres, delivering his final COP address before stepping down, expressed deep disappointment and accused powerful fossil‑fuel interests of distorting science and delaying action.  Delegates from oil‑producing nations, including Saudi Arabia’s Mohammad Ayoub, argued their historical emissions were relatively small and warned that a rapid shift away from fossil fuels could cause “fuel poverty.”  Russia cautioned against turning the debate into slogans.

## Voices of frustration
Climate advocates voiced outrage.  Former U.S. Vice‑President Al Gore called it “outrageous” that a handful of petro‑states could veto any mention of fossil fuels and urged a reform of the COP process to better reflect scientific urgency and global will.  The lack of a clear financial roadmap also spurred criticism from NGOs and developing‑country representatives, who fear the absence of firm numbers gives richer nations too much leeway.

The collapse of the COP31 political agreement mirrors the 2009 Copenhagen failure, underscoring how deep divisions over energy transition and finance continue to stall global climate action.  As the world looks ahead to the next summit, the pressure mounts on negotiators to bridge these gaps and deliver a deal that truly addresses the climate emergency.

sources.title: Longest-ever UN climate talks end with no deal as deep divisions exposed
